The Next Best Gen Z Product - Gummy Gains  
 
Group 6 - Carson Guise, Liam Miller 
Rochester Institute of Technology 
MKTG 365: Marketing Analytics 
Dr. Emi Moriuchi 
December 4th, 2025

2 
1. Executive Summary 
 
A large majority of Gen Z is in the midst of a shift towards a more active and 
health-conscious lifestyle. They care about spending their free time doing physical activities and 
eating healthily. According to ABC Fitness, 73% are members or users of health clubs, gyms, or 
studios, making Gen Z a profitable target for fitness and health brands (Rehfeldt, C., 2024). 
These healthy consumers also use supplements to better their active lifestyle, but it gets to the 
point where they have to spend a lot of money on various bottles of supplements and take each 
supplement one by one. Looking at Gen Z particularly, most of them are still in college, meaning 
they are very price-sensitive consumers who are looking for a cheap and effective alternative. 
That’s where Gummy Gains comes in: the low- cost customizable gummy supplement that 
allows you to spend less and choose what you want to put into your body.  
Through research, we found that for our consumers, price matters the most, followed by 
sweetness and flavor, and then contents. Our consumers are only looking for cheap supplements, 
and to make this a realistic goal, we offer ours between $15 and $20, a customizable and 
delicious alternative to their normal supplement intake. Data from our survey pointed us in the 
direction that we have two segments of customers, the “Price-Conscious” and the “Customizers” 
that both prioritize lower prices.   
Looking towards the strategic implications of our product in the market, management 
should look into the feasibility of including two supplements into one product scientifically, and 
once that is figured out, how they can include more supplements within one gummy to boost the 
customization of the product. Likewise, they should go about A/B testing both the sales process 
and marketing efforts to really understand what other features and benefits Gen Z is looking for. 
Gen Z offers a lot of potential buying power, being 56% of the market value of the 
health-conscious.  
 
2. Background and Business Context 
 
Our product is geared towards those looking to improve their health and wellness. Our 
product, Gummay Gains, falls into the dietary supplement category. Since the pandemic, 
supplements have become increasingly more popular in the U.S., and specifically with the 
younger generation. Personalized nutrition that is able to target an individual’s health goals is 
being sought after. Consumers have also shifted their mindsets from reactive healthcare to 
“preventative” healthcare. Moreover, the gummy form is becoming increasingly more popular 
(especially among the younger generation). Thus, we decided to distinguish our product by its 
gummy form, as supplements are traditionally sold in capsules or powder. According to Mordor 
Intelligence, the current market (2025) is USD 145.62 billion, and the projected market (2030) is 
USD 179.36 billion. The compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) for 2025-2030 is projected at 
4.62%. The shift to a preventative health care mindset will likely account for 1.2% of the 
projected CAGR. Some of the top competitors in the dietary supplement market include: Amway 
Corporation, Herbalife Ltd., Nestlé S.A., Bayer AG, and Haleon plc. These companies have 
started to integrate gummy supplements into their product segments, but the customization of 
these gummy supplements remains limited. 
Customers' needs in the supplement category revolve around maintaining their general 
well-being and health, as well as preventative healthcare, as mentioned previously. They’re

3 
looking to buy supplements that are transparent with their ingredients, as well as supplements 
that can be personalized to their needs and goals. According to Grand View Research, factors 
that affect buying decisions are most influenced by recommendations from health providers, 
convenience, and price. Factors like aging populations and increasing disposable income in 
developing economies are also major influences on the growth in the dietary supplement market 
(Mordor Intelligence). Consumers are also looking for supplements that target immune system 
enhancement, digestive health optimization, and nutritional deficiency prevention.  
The strategic question we hoped to answer during this survey was: “What do consumers 
value most when choosing gummy supplements?” Thus, the top of our survey emphasized this 
and also told respondents to “Please imagine you are purchasing a container of gummies (each 
container includes 50 supplements). Based on the features listed below, please select the 
combination you would most prefer.” 
​
From our competitors' and consumers' preferences, how can we create a product that’s 
distinguishable while also containing key features that consumers are looking for? How would 
we be able to simulate market response to alternative configurations of our product?  
 
3. Methodology Overview 
 
​
The type of conjoint we used was choice-based conjoint, making the respondents choose 
their preferred product over our four attributes and 15 levels. Respondents had to go through a 
series of questions that gave them three product profiles, and asked them which product profile 
they preferred the most. After completing this questionnaire, part of the survey, the respondents 
were asked a series of demographic questions. Specifically, we asked for their gender, age, 
education level, if they attend/attended RIT, employment status, and activity level. 
The attributes (4) and levels (15) we specified for this survey were price (low <$10, 
medium ($10-$25), high (>$25), contents (one supplement (predetermined), two supplements 
(predetermined), customizable supplements (can choose two supplements)), flavor (blue 
raspberry, cherry, orange, watermelon, mixed/assorted), and sweetness (low sugar (<5g), 
sugar-free (0g), mild sweetness (5-10g), extra sweet (>10g)). It is important to note that for 
contents, we specified that for both one and two supplements, the supplements are 
predetermined, and for customizable, the customers can pick two of their choice. 
For our target segment, we wanted to make sure that we were targeting U.S. Gen Z 
consumers (13-28 year olds) who are health-conscious. To get responses from our intended target 
audience, the two of us sent out this link to various groups. Liam sent it to the RIT baseball team, 
and Carson posted it on his social media. After the data collection, we obtained a sample size of 
35 students, allowing us to move forward with our analysis.  
For each question (11 in total), respondents of the survey had the choice between four 
different product profiles (or a none option) that had randomly selected levels from each 
attribute. An example question would give four choices with options such as: 1) low price 
(<$10), one supplement, watermelon, and a low sugar (<5g). 2) high price (>$25), customizable 
(can choose two supplements), blue raspberry, extra sweet (>10g). 3) medium price ($10-$25), 
two supplements (predetermined), mixed/assorted, sugar-free (0g). 4) low price (<$10), two 
supplements (predetermined), cherry, medium sweetness (5-10g). 5) None of the above. 
We used Hierarchical Bayes analysis to determine the partworth utility of each attribute. 
This analysis was done within Sawtooth, as they use hierarchical bayes to analyze the data.

4 
4. Key Findings 
 
 
After collecting our survey responses, we have concluded that the most important 
attribute of our product is price, followed by flavor and sweetness level, and lastly contents. This 
is consistent with our demographic of Gen Z, who are predominantly college students, due to the 
fact that many college students find themselves looking for the cheapest alternative option for 
things, making them very price-conscious consumers because they are already full-time students. 
From our respondents' data, we found that 80% are full-time students, meaning they may not 
have the time to work, or if they do, they can only work very few hours.

6 
Looking further at the specific attributes and what our respondents liked and didn’t like, 
we can see that for the most important attribute, price, low price (<$10) is the most important 
level with a utility of 52.3, while high price (>$25) is the least important level with a utility of 
-76.74. Moving to the next important attributes, for contents, respondents preferred the 
customizable supplements, with a utility of 27.67, and disliked the one supplement option, with a 
utility of -30.07. For flavor, respondents found the most utility in the Blue Raspberry flavor with 
30.31, and a dislike for cherry with a utility of -23.17. Lastly, for the least important attribute, 
sweetness, sugar-free (0g) was the most important level with a utility of 17.25, and extra sweet 
(>10g) was the least important level, with a utility of -33.9.  
Considering that our respondents are very conscious consumers, there are many 
trade-offs they were willing to make in order to fit their needs. One of the biggest tradeoffs we 
can see is with price. Respondents valued price the most, and further, a low price was essentially 
the deciding factor in which product they chose. We can see with the price utilities that the first 
option was low price (<$10), then medium price ($10 - $25), to lastly high price (>$25). This 
was the overarching deciding factor for most respondents, leaving them to care less about other 
attributes, like flavor and sweetness levels, to fit their needs.

From our data, we concluded that our best segmentation strategy would be to utilize two 
segments to efficiently market our product. With these two segments, we decided that segment 
one would be named the “Price-Conscious” and segment two would be named the 
“Customizers.” The Price-Conscious are 51.43% of our respondents (18), while our Customizers 
are the other 48.57% respondents (17). As seen by the segmentation done by Sawtooth, we can 
see there is a difference between the two. The Price-Conscious care about low price, 
customizable supplements, orange flavor, and sugar-free gummies, while the Customizers prefer 
low to mid price, customizable supplements, blue raspberry, and low sugar gummies. We believe 
that these two segments will allow us to effectively focus our marketing efforts. When we tried 
other segment numbers, such as three and four, there was a lot of overlap amongst the segments 
in terms of preferences, causing us to solidify two segments.

8 
 
 Note: Price Simulation within Sawtooth 
 
​
When considering the price sensitivity of our respondents, we simulated three different 
products with different prices (low (<$10), medium ($10 - $25), and high (>$25), with the top 
level of each other attribute (customizable supplements, blue raspberry flavor, and sugar-free 
(0g)). From this simulation, we can see that both segments prefer a low to medium price, with a 
share of preference of 78.7% for the low price for the Price-Conscious segment and 43.85% for 
the medium price for the Customizers segment. From this, we can conclude that our price point 
should be within the range of $10 to $25, and any price higher than that range is not feasible. 
Using this, we believe that we should price our product around $15 to ensure we are meeting the 
demand of both segments, as well as making our pricing realistic with manufacturing. It is 
important to note that with this product, the prices may vary depending on what supplements are 
included, because of the nature of their cost.  
 
5. Insights and Interpretation 
 
From our key findings, we can devise a strategy for the implication of our product into 
the fitness and wellness markets. Overall, our consumers are looking for something that is 
low-priced and customizable. We believe that Gummy Gains offers this to our customers in a

9 
way that satisfies the features they are looking for in a supplement brand, as well as various other 
benefits, such as convenience.  
​
Moving forward with the implication of the product, we believe we are in the right 
market due to the fact that the market size and value of the health-conscious can be attributed to 
56% of Gen Z (39,200,000). Recent trends within Gen Z have dictated that they care more about 
their fitness and health than other generations. Gen Z is looking at fitness and wellness with a 
holistic approach, meaning they care about all aspects of themselves: their mind, body, and their 
community (Rehfeldt, C., 2024). Our product satisfies their desire to take care of their body in an 
affordable, convenient, and delicious way. A study done in 2022 revealed that 40% of American 
adults have issues with swallowing pills, something our product inherently solves for them, as 
well as others just wanting to take their supplements (Mount Sinai Health System, 2022). Our 
brand should compete using this differentiator as the driving force of our marketing to highlight 
how we are different from other supplement brands. Various supplement brands can compete 
with us, such as Amway and Herbalife, but other brands cannot say they offer their products in 
gummy form, at a low price, and as customizable as ours.  
​
It is important to note that gummy forms of medication and supplements are something 
that is not new to the market. We are offering these supplements that are targeted towards the 
health-conscious Gen Z who are looking for a cheap and convenient way to stay on their health 
journey.  
 
6. Strategic Recommendations 
 
Looking towards a final product to launch, we are considering a line of low to 
medium-priced gummy supplements where customers can choose two supplements from a 
variety of them to build their own gummy supplement. We should plan to offer both a variety of 
flavors, with a heavy preference towards blue raspberry, as well as the choice between either 
sugar-free (0g) or low sugar (<5g). Our product will thrive because of its customizable features 
that allow consumers to get exactly what they want out of it, something a lot of Gen Z consumers 
are looking for. Emphasizing the low cost of this product is what is going to define our product 
strategy to build a successful product. 
​
To go further into pricing, we believe that a pricing strategy between $15 to $20 will 
ensure that we are catering towards our segments' desires, as well as meeting realistic 
manufacturing procedures. It is important to note that prices will vary depending on the 
supplements included in depending on the types of supplements they choose to include in their 
combination. For example, if the customer is including protein in their supplement combination, 
that is going to be higher priced at about $20, rather than if they picked a supplement 
combination with melatonin or caffeine. These containers will have 50 supplements in each.  
​
To market this effectively, we must position our product using our differentiating factors 
of low price and customization. In doing so, our messaging will be targeted towards the active 
and health-conscious Gen Z, utilizing buzzwords like low price and cheap, effective, and 
convenient. To better target both of our segments, for our Price-Conscious segment, we will put 
heavy emphasis on the low price, while for our Customizers, we will put heavy emphasis on the 
customization of the supplements. Some marketing techniques that would be useful for our brand 
are social media, digital marketing, influencer marketing (with small to mid-sized influencers), 
collaborations with college sports teams and college gyms, and word of mouth. To talk more

10 
about social media, we will want to focus on TikTok and Instagram as our main platforms, but 
also focus on other apps, such as Strava (a workout tracking app), and Snapchat. With these 
channels, we will be able to build trust with our consumers that our product works, causing 
consumers to want to try our product.  
 
7. Limitations and Considerations 
 
The first constraint of this study was the limited number of our sample size, n=35. This 
number is too small to generalize all of Gen Z’s dietary supplement preferences. The lack of 
representativeness due to the small sample size leads to an increased random error. When 
collecting data, our various sources may also present some biases. For example, this survey was 
sent out to the baseball team, which is a large niche group of people that could skew our results. 
A majority of our respondents (42.86%) answered that they play varsity sports. It’s also 
important to note that 54.29% of respondents answered that they attend RIT. Likewise, this 
survey was taken outside the scope of RIT students. With the respondents from the social media 
sites, there are a variety of students who participated in this survey from other colleges and 
universities. While this may have little swing in the results, it is important to note.  
We also underestimated the cost of this product. In our survey, we listed low prices as 
less than $10, but realistically, a low price for gummy vitamins would be between $10 and $15. 
Medium price would be between $15 and $25. The high price would be greater than $25. Our 
study also left out the possible supplements that we would be incorporating into our gummies. 
We left this out because we were unsure about the user customization feature of our gummies; 
mixing certain supplements may not be feasible or could possibly be dangerous to consumers. 
Although multivitamin gummy supplements are sold in the dietary supplement market, there is 
research done to ensure that these combinations are possible.  
Looking towards next steps for implementing our product into the market, there are many 
parts of the product we still need to test to ensure its feasibility and success. First, we should look 
at how the combination of supplements into one gummy might look, such as combining creatine 
and protein, caffeine and citrulline, or melatonin and magnesium. Once that is figured out, our 
company should look into providing more than two supplement options, branching out into three, 
four, or more supplements to capitalize on our differentiation point of customization. Ensuring 
these are scientifically able to be combined into one, as well as testing that people are supposed 
to take these at the same time, is something we need to test. Next, we should begin to conduct 
A/B testing of how our sales process should work, especially with the customizable supplements. 
Lastly, we will also need to A/B test our marketing efforts and messaging, especially on social 
media, to understand what our consumers like or dislike about our efforts.
